title: The moon keeps the calendar
hook: most Buddhist holy days fall on full and new moons; dates move each year

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the great collections, and your line was by kind and by number. Which two lines did you keep? Today a new part of the path opens: the festival year. Day six hundred eighty-one.

Ask a Buddhist friend in Sri Lanka or Thailand when Vesak is this year, and they might have to check. Not because they've forgotten. Because it moves. Last year it was one date, next year another, sometimes weeks apart. Holidays pinned to a calendar square don't work that way. But for the early Buddhists, the calendar wasn't a grid on the wall. It was in the sky. Look up on a clear night and you can read it: full, half, new. For the next sixteen days, we walk through the Buddhist year. And it starts, fittingly, with the moon. Today: uposatha.
screen: `WHEN IS VESAK THIS YEAR?` → `IT MOVES.` → `THE CALENDAR IN THE SKY.`

segments.voice: In the Buddha's India, time was kept by the moon. A month ran from one full moon or new moon to the next. And the texts show the monks gathering on certain moon days, the full moon and the new moon, and in time the half moons too. These are uposatha days, observance days. On the full and new moon, monks gather to recite their rules together, the patimokkha. And lay people come to the monastery, listen to teaching, and some keep extra precepts for the day. That rhythm still beats across much of the Buddhist world. In Sri Lanka, every full moon day, called poya, is a public holiday. Then the big festivals sit on particular full moons. Vesak on one. The first sermon on another. The end of the rains retreat on another. Because a lunar year of twelve months is about eleven days shorter than the solar year, the festivals slide earlier each year, and every few years an extra month is added to pull them back. So the dates move, but the moon stays the same. Not every tradition keeps the moon. Japan moved to the solar calendar in the eighteen-seventies, and Japanese temples now generally mark the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing on fixed solar dates. Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese communities generally keep the lunar dates. Different calendars, same stories. And one nice result of keeping the moon: anyone, anywhere, can look up and know roughly where they are in the holy year.
screen: `MONTHS FROM MOON TO MOON.` · `UPOSATHA: THE OBSERVANCE DAYS.` · `THE FESTIVALS SLIDE, THEN RESET.` · then, large: `THE MOON KEEPS THE CALENDAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find this year's full moons. Sit, and settle for a few breaths. Picture tonight's sky, and the moon wherever it is in its cycle. Is it waxing or waning? If you're not sure, that's fine. After the bell, look it up, or step outside tonight and see. Then find the next full moon and mark it. You might keep it as a quiet day: a little more stillness, a little more care. The bell holds the time.
uposatha. The Pali word for the observance day, kept on full and new moons, when most Buddhist holy days fall, so their dates move each year. Today's word.
Your line: look up, and know. Tonight, look for the moon, and say what phase it's in. Day six hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Across the Theravada world, lay Buddhists visit temples on full-moon and new-moon uposatha days, often keeping eight precepts, and monks recite the patimokkha on the full and new moons.

original.note: Pali uposatha: the observance day, kept on full and new moons (and half moons).

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhist holidays have fixed dates, like most holidays.
what it means: most follow the moon, so their dates move each year.
what a scholar hears: the uposatha may be older than Buddhism; the Vinaya says the Buddha adopted moon-day gatherings other religious groups already kept.

notes: Block G opens. Confirm Vinaya Mv 2 account that King Bimbisara suggested the monks gather on moon days as other ascetics did (trapdoor).
Confirm that the patimokkha is recited on full and new moon days only (not half moons).
Japan adopted the Gregorian calendar in 1873; practice of fixed solar dates (April 8, Dec 8, Feb 15) varies by temple, some use a one-month-later date.
